questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Boundary line of a linear inequality
questions.learningObjective: identify the boundary of a region described by a linear inequality
questions.stem: The inequality 3x + 2y <= 12 describes a region. What is its boundary line?

options.text: The set of points where 3x + 2y is at most 12
options.misconception: treats an inequality as though it named a set of equality points

options.text: The set of points where 3x plus 2y minus 12 changes sign
options.misconception: describes the sign change rather than the set of equality points

options.text: The set of points where 3x + 2y equals 12
The set of points where 3x + 2y is less than 12
options.misconception: confuses the whole half-plane with its edge

questions.explanation: The boundary is the set of points where the two sides are equal, that is where 3x + 2y - 12 is 0, which is the straight line y = 6 - 1.5x. The points (0, 6), (4, 0) and (2, 3) all satisfy it, each giving 12, while (0, 0) gives 0 and (1, 1) gives 5, so neither of those is on the line. The inequality itself picks out a whole side of that line, not the line.
questions.hint: The boundary is where the two sides of the inequality are equal.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Strict and non-strict boundary lines
questions.learningObjective: decide whether a boundary line is drawn solid or dashed
questions.stem: How should the boundary of 3x + 2y <= 12 be drawn, compared with the boundary of 3x + 2y < 12?

options.text: Both boundaries are solid, because a line is drawn the same either way
options.misconception: thinks the drawing style is unrelated to the sign of the inequality

options.text: Both are dashed, because the line itself is the same set of points
options.misconception: notices the line is shared but misses that inclusion changes the drawing

options.text: The solid boundary becomes dashed, because the endpoints are excluded
options.misconception: confuses which set is the boundary with which points are excluded

options.text: The strict one is dashed and the other solid, because equality is included only in the second

questions.explanation: A solid line says every point on it is part of the region, and a dashed line says the points on it are left out. The non-strict sign allows equality, so (4, 0) belongs and the line is solid, while the strict sign excludes equality, so the same point fails and the line is dashed. The line itself is unchanged, and the two regions differ only on it.
questions.hint: Decide whether points on the line belong to the region before drawing it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Test point used to choose a shaded side
questions.learningObjective: use a test point to decide which side of a boundary to shade
questions.stem: Which point can be used to decide which side of the line 3x + 2y = 12 to shade for the inequality 3x + 2y <= 12?

options.text: (10, 0), because it is far from the line and easy to see
options.misconception: picks a point that lies on the wrong side, so the shading is decided wrongly

options.text: (0, 0), because it satisfies the inequality and is easy to check
(1, 1), because it is close to the line
options.misconception: chooses a point on the correct side but for the wrong reason, proximity to the line

options.text: (2, 3), because it lies on the boundary itself
options.misconception: uses a boundary point, which satisfies the non-strict form for a misleading reason

questions.explanation: Any point that is clearly not on the line will do, provided its status is easy to check. At (0, 0) the left side is 0, which is at most 12, so that point is inside and the shading goes on its side. By contrast (10, 0) gives 30 and (0, 10) gives 20, both outside, so a test point chosen from those would shade the wrong side. A point exactly on the line is a poor choice because it tells you nothing about either side.
questions.hint: Pick a point you can evaluate quickly and that is clearly not on the line.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Rewriting an inequality in slope-intercept form
questions.learningObjective: put a linear inequality into slope-intercept form without changing its meaning
questions.stem: The inequality 3x - 2y > 6 is rewritten in slope-intercept form. Which form is equivalent?

options.misconception: drops the factor of one half on the slope
reverses the direction without any reason when solving for y
divides by a positive number but forgets the sign on the left

questions.explanation: Move the constant first to get 3x - 2y > 6 into 3x - 2y > 6, then divide by 2 to get 1.5x - y > 3, then add y. Dividing by -2 is what reverses the direction, so the result is y < 1.5x - 3. Testing a point confirms it: (4, 2) satisfies the original since 12 - 4 = 8 > 6, and in the rewritten form 2 < 1.5 times 4 minus 3, which is 3, so it still holds.
questions.hint: Watch the sign of the number you divide by, since it decides the direction.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Reversal caused by dividing by a negative
questions.learningObjective: apply the reversal rule when solving an inequality by dividing by a negative
questions.stem: The inequality -2y > 10 is solved for y. Which result is right?

options.misconception: divides by a negative but forgets that the direction must reverse
divides by -2 but forgets that both the value and the direction change
keeps the direction but loses the sign of the constant as well

questions.explanation: Dividing by -2 gives 10 over -2, which is -5, and dividing by a negative number swaps the two sides of the inequality, so the result is y < -5. Checking the two cases shows why the reversal matters: y = 4 fails the correct form but satisfies y > -5, while y = -6 satisfies the correct form and fails the other. The two forms therefore pick out opposite sets of values.
questions.hint: Ask what value the divisor has, and whether it is positive.

questions.topic: Negating an inequality statement
questions.learningObjective: write the negation of a one-variable inequality
questions.stem: Which statement is the negation of the inequality x + 3 < 8?

options.misconception: negates the sign but leaves the strict form in place
restates the original instead of denying it
keeps the weak sign, which is not a negation of a strict one

questions.explanation: Negating means saying the original is false, so the sign flips and the strictness flips with it: less than becomes at least. The pair partitions every input, since exactly one of x + 3 < 8 and x + 3 >= 8 holds for any x. Testing confirms it: x = 4 is in the original only and x = 5 is in the negation only.

questions.topic: A system of inequalities as simultaneous conditions
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a point feasible for a system of inequalities
questions.stem: A point is called feasible for a system of inequalities when which condition holds?

options.text: At least one of the inequalities is satisfied
options.misconception: treats a system like a choice rather than a set of requirements

options.text: Every inequality in the system is satisfied
Every inequality is satisfied strictly, with no equality allowed
options.misconception: insists on strictness even where the system allows equality

options.text: The point lies on the boundary of the system
options.misconception: picks out the boundary rather than the interior

questions.explanation: A system is a list of requirements that must all be met at once, so a point qualifies only if it satisfies every entry. For the system 3x + 2y <= 12 and x + 2y <= 8, the point (2, 3) gives 12 and 8 and so passes both, while (3, 3) gives 15 and 9 and fails both. Satisfying only one condition is not enough, which is what separates a system from a choice between conditions.
questions.hint: A system is a list of requirements, not a menu of choices.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Intersection of two half-planes
questions.learningObjective: find the corner points of a region cut out by two linear constraints
questions.stem: The region defined by x >= 0, y >= 0, 3x + 2y <= 12 and x + 2y <= 8 is a quadrilateral. What are its corner points?

options.misconception: reads the intercepts off the wrong pair of lines
takes the x-intercept of the wrong line, 8 instead of 4
pairs the intercepts with the wrong crossing point

questions.explanation: A corner sits where two boundary lines cross and the point is still inside. On the x-axis the tighter of the two lines is 3x = 12, giving (4, 0), and on the y-axis the tighter is 2y = 8, giving (0, 4). The two slanted lines meet where subtracting one from the other gives 2x = 4, so x = 2 and y = 3. Together with the origin that is the four corners, and (5, 0) is outside because 15 exceeds 12.
questions.hint: Find the crossings of the boundary lines and keep the ones that fit.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Corner where two boundary lines cross
questions.learningObjective: identify the role of the point where two boundary lines cross
questions.stem: Two boundary lines cross at the point (2, 3). What does that point represent for the region they bound?

options.text: A corner point, provided it satisfies every other constraint as well
A corner point, because two lines always produce one
options.misconception: assumes a crossing is automatically part of the region

options.text: The centre of the region, since it lies on both lines
options.misconception: reads a crossing as a midpoint of the whole region

options.text: A point on the boundary only, never a corner of the region
options.misconception: believes a corner can never sit on two boundaries at once

questions.explanation: Where two constraints are exactly met at the same time, the region changes from one active side to another, and that point is a corner, provided every remaining condition is also met. For 3x + 2y <= 12 and x + 2y <= 8 the crossing is at (2, 3), which gives 12 and 8 and satisfies the two sign conditions, so it is one of the four corners. A crossing that fell outside another constraint would not belong to the region at all.
questions.hint: Two conditions met at once is what makes a corner, provided the rest still hold.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Feasibility of a candidate point
questions.learningObjective: test whether a point is feasible for a system of inequalities
questions.stem: Is the point (3, 3) feasible for the system x >= 0, y >= 0, 3x + 2y <= 12 and x + 2y <= 8?

options.text: Yes, because both of its coordinates are positive
options.misconception: checks only the sign conditions and ignores the two budgets

options.text: No, because it breaks both of the budget conditions
No, but only because it breaks one of the sign conditions
options.misconception: gives the right verdict for the wrong reason

options.text: Yes, because 3x + 2y equals 15, which is close to 12
options.misconception: accepts a value merely because it is near the limit

questions.explanation: Every condition has to be checked, not just the easy ones. At (3, 3) the sign conditions pass, but 3x + 2y is 9 + 6 = 15, which exceeds 12, and x + 2y is 3 + 6 = 9, which exceeds 8, so both budgets are broken. Two failures make the point infeasible even though neither coordinate is negative, which is the point of a system.
questions.hint: Substitute the point into every condition, not only the easy ones.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Extreme value of a linear objective at a corner
questions.learningObjective: locate the greatest value of a linear quantity over a region
questions.stem: The quantity P = 4x + 3y is to be made as large as possible inside the region x >= 0, y >= 0, 3x + 2y <= 12, x + 2y <= 8. Where is the greatest value found?

options.text: At the origin, since the region starts there
options.misconception: assumes the origin is always the best point

options.text: On the edge between (0, 0) and (4, 0)
options.misconception: picks an edge rather than one of its end points

options.text: At the corner (2, 3), where P is 17
At the corner (0, 4), where P is 12
options.misconception: stops at the first corner that looks tallest on a sketch

questions.explanation: A linear quantity grows along any straight direction, so over a region with corners it can be pushed higher and higher until it reaches a corner and can go no further. Evaluating P at all four corners gives 0 at (0, 0), 12 at (0, 4), 17 at (2, 3) and 16 at (4, 0), so the greatest is 17 at (2, 3). A scan of the whole region confirms that no other point does better.
questions.hint: A linear quantity improves as you move in a suitable direction, so it peaks at a corner.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Non-negative constraints in a counting model
questions.learningObjective: explain what non-negative constraints contribute to a counting model
questions.stem: A club models numbers of items with x and y. What does the pair of conditions x >= 0 and y >= 0 add?

options.text: That the two variables sum to zero
options.misconception: reads two separate conditions as one joint condition

options.text: An upper bound on each variable
options.misconception: reads sign conditions as size limits

options.text: That both variables are at most zero
options.misconception: drops the equality case that the weak sign allows

options.text: A lower bound of zero on each variable

questions.explanation: A weak sign with zero on the right admits the boundary, so x >= 0 allows every value from 0 upwards and rules out negatives. In a counting model that is exactly what is needed, because a negative number of items has no meaning, and the point (0, 0) is still allowed as the case of buying nothing. Nothing about the size of either variable is bounded from above by these two conditions.
questions.hint: Ask what a negative count would mean, and then what the conditions permit.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Bounded feasible region
questions.learningObjective: explain what it means for a region to be bounded
questions.stem: Why is the region x >= 0, y >= 0, 3x + 2y <= 12, x + 2y <= 8 called a bounded region?

options.text: No point in it has an x or y value above a fixed limit
Its boundary consists of exactly four straight pieces
options.misconception: confuses bounded with the number of edges

options.text: Every point in it has whole-number coordinates
options.misconception: confuses bounded with a lattice

options.text: It contains a corner at the origin
options.misconception: thinks one corner is enough to bound a region

questions.explanation: Bounded means there is a largest possible value for each variable, not that the region has a particular shape. Since 3x + 2y <= 12 forces 3x <= 12 and 2y <= 12, the x values can never pass 4 and the y values can never pass 6, so the region is trapped inside a finite box. The point (2, 3) still lies inside that box, so the bound is not vacuous.
questions.hint: Bounded means each variable has a greatest possible value.

questions.topic: Unbounded feasible region
questions.learningObjective: recognise a region that is not trapped inside a finite box
questions.stem: Consider the region x >= 0 together with y <= 2x. What can be said about it?

options.text: It is unbounded, since x can grow without limit
It is bounded, because the two lines meet at a single point
options.misconception: assumes two lines always enclose a region

options.text: It is bounded, because y is at most twice x
options.misconception: reads a relation between two variables as a bound on each

options.text: It is empty, because the conditions contradict each other
options.misconception: fails to find the feasible point at the origin

questions.topic: At most and at least phrasing
questions.learningObjective: translate an at most or at least phrase into an inequality
questions.stem: A van can carry at most 40 kg. Which inequality states that condition correctly?

options.misconception: drops the boundary, so a load of exactly 40 is wrongly excluded
reverses the direction of the bound
reads a maximum as a strict lower bound

questions.explanation: At most means the value is not allowed to exceed the limit, so it becomes the weak inequality w <= 40, which admits 40 itself and excludes 41. At least would become w >= 40, admitting 40 and excluding 39. A strict sign is wrong here because a load of exactly 40 kg is allowed, and the brief phrase fewer than 40 would be the wording that genuinely requires a strict sign.

options.misconception: counts only the whole-number points lying on the boundary line
counts the pairs on the boundary line and forgets the ones below it
counts a full square of whole numbers without applying the budget at all

questions.explanation: Fix x and count the y values that fit. At x = 0 there are 11 choices of y, from 0 to 10, at x = 1 there are 9, then 7, then 5, then 3, and at x = 5 there is only y = 0, so 1 choice. Adding the column sizes 11 + 9 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 gives 36. The side to the left of the vertical line x = 3
options.misconception: reads a greater-than sign as though the shaded side were the smaller values

options.text: The line itself, with nothing on either side
options.misconception: confuses the boundary with the whole solution set

options.misconception: believes a boundary makes the two sides equally included

questions.topic: Points exactly on a boundary line

options.misconception: puts the y values in the wrong order, swapping 2 and 3

options.text: (2, 3) alone, since the other two lie on the axes
options.misconception: excludes axis points, which are perfectly good points of the line
inserts the odd values of y that do not give a whole number

adds the two coefficients instead of applying them to the coordinates

A second route that flags every lattice point at which two conditions are tight returns the same four points, which confirms the count.
questions.hint: Count the points at which two conditions are met at exactly the same time.

questions.stem: Among the four corner points of the region x >= 0, y >= 0, 3x + 2y <= 12 and x + 2y <= 8 is the point (0, 4). What is the value of 4x + 3y there? Report the number only.

That corner is worth checking against the others, since 4x + 3y at (2, 3) is 17 and at (4, 0) is 16, so 12 is the smallest of the four values rather than the largest.

questions.topic: Area of a region from its corner points

questions.stem: Draw the diagonal from the origin to the opposite corner and split the shape into two triangles to find its area in square units. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Draw the diagonal from (0, 0) to (2, 3) and the region splits into two triangles. The first has vertices (0, 0), (4, 0) and (2, 3), with area 4 times 3 over 2, that is 6, and the second has vertices (0, 0), (2, 3) and (0, 4), with area 2 times 4 over 2, that is 4, so the total is 10. The shoelace formula on the four corners in boundary order gives 10 as well, which confirms the figure. Corners alone are enough because the region is convex and so has no need to be split any further.

questions.topic: Best whole-number value when the continuous optimum is fractional

questions.stem: A region is given by x >= 0, y >= 0, 3x + 2y <= 12 and 2x + 3y <= 11, and the quantity 3x + 4y is to be made as large as possible using whole numbers only. What is the greatest value available? Report the number only.

Listing the whole-number points that fit both budgets and testing each shows the best is (1, 3), giving 15, and the next best is (2, 2) giving 14. The corner (0, 4) must be rejected because 3 times 4 is 12, which exceeds 11, so the whole-number answer is 15 rather than 16.

questions.topic: x-coordinate of a corner from two equations

questions.explanation: Subtracting x + y = 5 from 2x + 3y = 12 leaves x + 2y = 7, and subtracting x + y = 5 from that again leaves y = 2. Putting y = 2 into x + y = 5 gives x = 3, so the crossing is at (3, 2). Both lines are satisfied there, giving 6 + 6 = 12 and 3 + 2 = 5, and the point is inside the region since both budgets are met exactly.

questions.stem: A stall sells small items for 3 pounds each and large items for 5 pounds each. It may spend at most 17 pounds, and must sell at least 3 small and at least 2 large items. Which system of inequalities describes the plans that are allowed?

options.misconception: turns the minimum number of small items into a maximum
reads the 3 pounds as the price of a large item and 2 pounds of a small one
raises the budget so that unaffordable plans slip in

questions.explanation: The budget is spent as 3x + 2y, because x counts the 3-pound items and y counts the 2-pound ones, and at most 17 pounds means at most rather than at least. The wording at least 3 small items becomes x >= 3 and at least 2 large items becomes y >= 2. 0 at the origin, 18 at (0, 6), 25 at (3, 4) and 21 at (7, 0)
options.misconception: applies the coefficient 3 to the y-intercept instead of 4

options.text: It is inside the region, because both coordinates are non-negative
options.misconception: checks the sign conditions and ignores both budgets

options.misconception: believes the sign conditions alone can close a region

options.misconception: thinks corners require parallel boundaries

On the y-axis the first budget would allow 6 and the second 7, so the corner is (0, 6), while on the x-axis the first allows 9 and the second 7, so the corner is (7, 0). The two budgets cross at (3, 4), and with the origin that makes four corners, so the region is a quadrilateral.

negates the slope as well as the direction
inverts the 3 over 4 instead of simplifying it

Find where each pair of boundary lines crosses
Keep the intersection points that satisfy every condition

options.misconception: objects to drawing the boundary rather than to how it is drawn

questions.explanation: A solid line tells the reader that every point on it is inside the region, which is exactly what a strict sign denies. At (4, 0) the left side is exactly 12, so the point fails 3x + 2y < 12 while satisfying the weak form, and the same is true of every whole-number point on that line, namely (0, 6), (2, 3) and (4, 0). A dashed line is what keeps the boundary out.
questions.hint: Decide first whether points on the line are meant to be included.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Direction not reversed after dividing by a negative
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a missed reversal when dividing an inequality by a negative number
questions.stem: A student solves -2y > 10 and writes y > -5, then tests y = 4 and finds it works. What is wrong?

options.text: The direction was not reversed, so the accepted set is the mirror image of the correct one
The direction was not reversed, and the constant should also have kept its sign
options.misconception: blames two things when only the direction is wrong

options.text: The division was correct, but a strict sign becomes a weak one when a variable is isolated
options.misconception: confuses a division with an equality

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since testing y = 4 confirms the student's answer
options.misconception: accepts a value that only satisfies the mis-derived inequality

questions.explanation: Dividing by a negative number swaps the two sides of the inequality, so the correct result is y < -5, and testing y = 4 then correctly fails. The student's y = -5 came out right while the direction did not, and that combination selects the opposite set of values: y = 4 satisfies the mistake and fails the truth, while y = -6 satisfies the truth and fails the mistake. Testing a value the student already believes in cannot detect this slip.
questions.hint: Check the sign of the divisor before trusting the direction you kept.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Maximum claimed at a point that is not a corner
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an optimum claimed at a point that is not in the region
questions.stem: A student claims that the greatest value of 4x + 3y in the region x >= 0, y >= 0, 3x + 2y <= 12, x + 2y <= 8 is 18, at the point (3, 2). What is the error?

options.text: The point (3, 2) is in the region, but the value there is 17 and not 18
options.misconception: accepts the point and quibbles about the arithmetic only

options.text: The value 18 is right, but the corner that gives it is (4, 0)
options.misconception: keeps the value and moves it to a corner that gives 16

options.text: The point (3, 2) is on the boundary, so it cannot be the best choice
options.misconception: believes a boundary point is automatically excluded

options.text: The point (3, 2) is not in the region, since 3x + 2y is 13 there, which exceeds 12

questions.explanation: Every candidate has to pass the feasibility test first, and at (3, 2) the left side is 3 times 3 plus 2 times 2, which is 13, exceeding the limit of 12, so the point is outside the region entirely. Evaluating the four real corners gives 0, 12, 17 and 16, so the greatest value is 17 at (2, 3), and a scan of the whole region agrees. The 18 in the student's answer is 4 times 3 plus 3 times 2, which is an evaluation at a point that was never available.
questions.hint: A point has to be inside the region before its value means anything.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Why a linear objective is extreme at a corner
questions.learningObjective: explain why a linear quantity is extreme at a corner of a region
questions.stem: Explain why the greatest value of a linear quantity such as 4x + 3y over a region is found at a corner point rather than anywhere inside the region.

answer.exemplar: Move a little way from any point that is not a corner in some direction and the value cannot fail to increase. Concretely, at an interior point of the region both coordinates can be increased a little while staying inside, and since the coefficients 4 and 3 are positive, increasing the coordinates increases the value. So no interior point can be a greatest one. The same argument works on an edge, because along an edge one coordinate can always be moved in the direction that raises the value, and the coefficients cannot both vanish. The movement has to stop somewhere, and it stops exactly where a further move would break a condition, that is, where two conditions are met at equality at once. Those points are the corners, which is why a linear quantity is checked only at them. For the region x >= 0, y >= 0, 3x + 2y <= 12, x + 2y <= 8 the corners are (0, 0), (0, 4), (2, 3) and (4, 0), and 4x + 3y at them is 0, 12, 17 and 16, so the greatest is 17 at (2, 3).

questions.explanation: The stem asks for a reason, and the reason is that a linear quantity keeps improving as one moves in a suitable direction, so the best point cannot be in the interior or in the middle of an edge. The worked case is not decoration: it shows the four values and confirms that the largest of them is the answer rather than an assumption.
questions.hint: Ask whether the point could be improved by moving a little in some direction.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Why an inequality is drawn as a half-plane
questions.learningObjective: explain why a two-variable inequality gives a half-plane rather than a line
questions.stem: Explain why the solution set of an inequality in two variables is drawn as a half-plane with a boundary line, and not as just the line.

answer.exemplar: An inequality such as 3x + 2y <= 12 is a statement about every ordered pair of values, not about one special pair. Substituting any pair into the left side produces a number, and the inequality says that number must be at most 12. The pairs for which it is exactly 12 form a straight line, and those pairs are the boundary. The pairs for which it is less are all on one side of that line, and the pairs for which it is more are all on the other side, because the expression 3x + 2y grows steadily as the point moves away from the line in a given direction. So the solution set splits into the line itself plus one open side, which together make a half-plane. The line is drawn solid or dashed according to whether equality is allowed, and the strict inequality 3x + 2y < 12 leaves out the points of the line, such as (4, 0), where the left side is exactly 12.

questions.explanation: The stem asks why the shape is a region and not a curve, and the answer is that the inequality is a condition on every pair of values, with the equality cases forming only its edge. The final sentence is the part that is often missed, namely that the boundary is part of the answer only for a weak sign.
questions.hint: Compare the equality points with the points on either side of the line.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: How a worded problem becomes a system of inequalities
questions.learningObjective: explain how the clauses of a worded problem translate into a system of inequalities
questions.stem: A club must buy at least 3 small items and at least 2 large items, may spend at most 17 pounds, and prices the small items at 3 pounds and the large ones at 2 pounds. Describe how the wording becomes a system of inequalities, and say which whole-number plans it allows.

answer.exemplar: Each clause of the wording becomes one condition. Let x be the number of small items and y the number of large ones. The spending clause says the cost, which is 3x + 2y, must not exceed 17, giving 3x + 2y <= 17, and the weak sign is right because spending exactly 17 pounds is allowed. The clause about small items gives x >= 3 and the clause about large items gives y >= 2, both weak for the same reason. Any extra condition, such as a cap on one item, would add a further line. Listing the whole-number plans that satisfy all three gives (3, 2) costing 13, (3, 3) costing 15, (3, 4) costing 17, and (4, 2) costing 16, and no others, because (4, 3) would cost 18 and x = 5 leaves no room for the two large items that are required. If the quantity 4x + 5y is to be maximised, these four plans give 22, 27, 32 and 26, so the best is 32 at (3, 4), which spends the budget exactly.

questions.explanation: The stem asks for the translation and then for the consequences, so the one-to-one mapping from clause to condition has to be made explicit, including why the weak signs are right. The enumeration is the part that shows the translation is usable, and the closing objective is what the system is normally built for.
questions.hint: Match each clause to one condition, then test the plans it allows.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Why a whole-number answer can differ from the continuous one
questions.learningObjective: explain why a whole-number optimum can fall short of the continuous optimum
questions.stem: A fraction of a point cannot be bought. The region x >= 0, y >= 0, 3x + 2y <= 12 and 2x + 3y <= 11 has its best corner for 3x + 4y at (2.8, 1.8), giving 15.6. Explain why the answer to a problem that counts items is 15 and not 15.6.

answer.exemplar: The point (2.8, 1.8) is the crossing of the two budget lines, and there 3x + 4y is 15.6, which is the greatest value over the whole region if any real value of x and y is allowed. A count of items, however, is a whole number, and 2.8 small items and 1.8 large items are not quantities that can be bought, so the point is not an available plan. The available plans are the whole-number points inside the region, and testing each shows that (1, 3) gives 15 while (2, 2) gives 14 and (4, 0) gives 12, so 15 is the best that can actually be achieved. The corner (0, 4) must not be used even though 3x + 4y there is 16, because 2x + 3y at that point is 12, which exceeds the limit of 11. This is the usual situation in planning problems: the corner method locates the best continuous plan, and the whole-number rule then forces a small sacrifice, here three fifths of a unit.

questions.explanation: The stem asks for the difference between two answers, and the difference is exactly the whole-number restriction, which the explanation has to connect to the point that fractional counts are meaningless. The tempting wrong answer, 16 from the corner (0, 4), is dealt with explicitly because that corner is not even feasible, and the final figure makes the size of the sacrifice concrete.
questions.hint: Ask whether the winning corner can be bought in whole numbers.
